title: Fitting new cane webbing in a chair back
subtitle: Soak, stretch, and press sheet cane webbing into the routed groove of a chair back or seat opening, using a reed spline to lock it in place
excerpt: How to replace the woven cane panel in a chair back or seat. Covers removing the old spline and cane, cleaning the groove, soaking the new cane, tensioning it over the opening, driving in the reed spline, trimming the excess, and drying.
sourceNotes: Traditional cane and rush chair seating practice, public domain. UK furniture restoration trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pre-woven flat sheets of rattan cane in a hexagonal or other woven pattern. Sold by the metre in widths from 300 mm to 600 mm. It is fitted wet (after soaking for 20 to 30 minutes) which makes it flexible and allows it to be stretched taut over an opening. On drying, the cane tightens and firms up to a rigid, springy surface.

A flat strip of rattan or bamboo cut to match the width of the routed groove in the chair frame. It is hammered over the cane webbing edges into the groove to trap and lock the cane in place. The spline is typically 4 to 6 mm wide and matches the groove depth of the chair; an incorrectly sized spline will not hold the cane securely.

to trap the edges. INTERMEDIATE: soaking the cane and keeping even tension while the spline goes in are the skills that determine the quality of the final panel.
Remove the old spline and cane

Use a utility knife to cut along the top of the old spline around the full perimeter of the groove. Prize the spline out with a narrow screwdriver. Pull the old cane out of the groove and discard. Clean any old glue or cane residue from the groove walls with the utility knife tip or a narrow chisel. The groove must be clean for the new spline to sit at the correct depth.
Measure and soak the new cane

Cut the cane webbing to cover the full opening with at least 30 mm overhang on each side. Submerge the cane in warm water for 20 to 30 minutes until fully flexible. Keep it wet during fitting: wrap unused sections in a damp cloth.

Lay the wet cane over the opening, centering it so the weave pattern is straight and symmetrical. Use wedges of the spline material or short wooden dowels to temporarily hold the cane in the groove at the centre of each side while you tension the full panel. Pull gently from the opposite sides in turn to keep the tension even.

Apply a thin bead of wood glue into the groove around the full perimeter. Starting at one side, press the spline down into the groove over the cane using the rubber mallet, tapping progressively along the spline length. Work each side in sequence, keeping the cane taut as the spline goes in. At the corners, mitre the spline ends or bend the spline around the curve where the groove is rounded.

Once the spline is fully driven home, trim the excess cane around the perimeter using the utility knife, cutting flush with the outer edge of the spline. Allow the cane to dry at room temperature for at least two days before using the chair. As it dries the cane contracts, drawing the panel tighter and firmer.

attrs.symptom: Cane panel sags in the centre after drying
attrs.cause: The cane was not sufficiently tensioned before the spline was driven in, or the spline did not hold the cane edges firmly.
attrs.fix: Wet the panel thoroughly with a sponge and allow the moisture to tighten the cane. If this does not resolve the sag, remove the spline and re-do the fitting with better tension.

attrs.symptom: Spline splits or cracks when hammered into the groove
attrs.cause: The spline is too dry and brittle, or is wider than the groove.
attrs.fix: Soak the spline in water for 10 minutes before fitting to make it more flexible. Check the spline width against the groove before ordering.
